Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
Short definitions first
- “Copy” (for spells or abilities): putting a copy of that spell or ability onto the stack; a copy of a spell or ability is itself a spell or ability on the stack and copies characteristics and decisions (including targets) made for the original. A copy is not cast (it was put on the stack) and choices normally made on resolution are not copied. [707.10]
- “Cast a spell”: take a card from the zone it’s in (usually your hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs; that process makes it a spell on the stack. Copies placed on the stack are not cast. [601.2i][112.1a]

What happens in your sequence
1) Casting Emrakul created the “When you cast this spell…” triggered ability and put that triggered ability on the stack (that’s the normal cast trigger). [Emrakul, the Promised End]
2) You used Lithoform Engine to copy that triggered ability on the stack. Lithoform’s ability copies a triggered ability that’s on the stack and creates another instance of that ability on the stack; the copy can have new targets if Lithoform’s ability allows choosing new targets. The copy is a separate triggered ability on the stack. [Lithoform Engine ruling #3][Lithoform Engine]
- Each resolving instance of that triggered ability will apply its full effect (gain control of the targeted opponent during that player’s next turn, and after that turn that player takes an extra turn). Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other; the last one to be created is the one that actually grants control. Multiple such abilities can still each produce their “extra turn” effect. So copying the trigger means you will have two triggered-ability instances that each create an extra turn, but the most-recently created control effect is the one that governs who you actually control during that next turn. [707.10][Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]
3) When you untapped Lithoform and used it to copy the Emrakul permanent spell on the stack, Lithoform created a copy of the permanent spell on the stack (the copy is not cast). Lithoform’s permanent-spell copy is created on the stack and, when it resolves, becomes a token with the characteristics of that spell. Creating that copy does not count as casting the spell and therefore does not cause “When you cast this spell” triggers to be put on the stack. Also, for permanent spells Lithoform’s ruling notes you can’t choose new targets (if the permanent spell would have targets). [Lithoform Engine ruling #5][Lithoform Engine ruling #6][111.13]

Direct answers
- How many of your opponent’s turns do you control? You will control that opponent for their next turn only once: the last-created player-controlling effect (the most recently created triggered-ability instance) is the one that grants control; earlier-created control effects that affect the same player are overwritten. However, because both triggered-ability instances still create their “extra turn” effects, you will get an extra turn for each resolving instance. [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14][707.10]
- Do you get a second Emrakul? Yes — copying the permanent spell with Lithoform puts a copy on the stack that, when it resolves, becomes a token permanent with Emrakul’s characteristics. That gives you a second Emrakul entering the battlefield (a token). [Lithoform Engine ruling #5][111.13]
- Does copying the Emrakul spell give you another control-a-turn trigger? No — the copy of the Emrakul spell is not cast, so it does not create a “When you cast this spell” trigger. Creating the copy won’t cause cast triggers to be generated. The only extra control-trigger you got was the copy of the already-existing triggered ability you made earlier with Lithoform. [Lithoform Engine ruling #6][601.2i][112.1a]

Short practical summary you can act on: you will control your opponent for their next turn once (the latest-created control effect wins), you will get two extra turns afterward (one per triggered-ability instance you resolved), you end up with a second Emrakul token, and copying the spell itself does not produce another “when you cast” control trigger.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Short answer: Yes — if a card is exiled with Mimic Vat when each resolving instance of the ability resolves, you will get two token copies (one from each resolving instance).

Explanation and key definitions
- "Copy an ability": Putting a copy of an activated or triggered ability onto the stack; the copy is itself an ability and is placed on the stack as a separate instance (see [707.10]).
- What happens here: You activate Mimic Vat’s {3},{T} ability; that activated ability is an ability on the stack. If you use Lithoform Engine to copy that activated ability, Lithoform puts another instance of that ability onto the stack (Lithoform Engine ruling #3), and the copy’s source is the same source (the same Mimic Vat) as the original (Lithoform Engine ruling #0 and [707.10]).
- Each instance of the ability resolves separately. When an instance resolves it follows its text: “Create a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with this artifact…” The token created will be a copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat at the time that particular instance resolves (Mimic Vat ruling #4).
- If no card is exiled with Mimic Vat by the time an instance resolves, that instance creates no token (Mimic Vat ruling #6).
- If the exiled object is a melded permanent (so two cards are exiled), when an instance resolves you choose which of the exiled cards to copy (Mimic Vat ruling #1 and the rule about actions on “a” card, [607.3]).

Practical outcomes
- If a single card is exiled with Mimic Vat when both the original and the Lithoform copy resolve, you get two tokens, both copies of that exiled card.
- If the card exiled with Mimic Vat changes between the first resolution and the second, each token will be a copy of whatever is exiled at that resolution (they can be different — Mimic Vat ruling #4).
- If nothing is exiled with Mimic Vat when an instance resolves, that instance creates no token (Mimic Vat ruling #6).

Zones/objects named: the abilities are on the stack; the cards to be copied are in exile (the cards exiled with Mimic Vat); tokens are created onto the battlefield when each ability resolves.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
Short definitions (from the provided rules):
- X: a numeric placeholder in a spell’s mana cost that the spell’s controller chooses when casting the spell unless some effect defines X otherwise (see 107.3b).
- Total cost: the mana cost (or alternative cost) plus cost increases minus cost reductions; that finalized number is what you must pay to cast the spell (see 601.2f and the “Total Cost” definition).

What happens when you try to cast Awaken the Woods ({X}{G}{G}) with an opponent’s untapped Trinisphere plus a permanent that reduces your green spells’ cost by {1}:
1) Order of calculation: start with the spell’s mana cost ({X}{G}{G}), apply any cost increases, then apply your cost reduction, then apply Trinisphere’s effect if the spell’s mana component is less than three (per Trinisphere ruling #0 and 601.2f).

2) If you choose X = 0: the spell’s pre-reduction cost is {G}{G} (two green mana). After your −{1} cost effect and then Trinisphere is applied, the final total mana required will be three mana (Trinisphere forces spells that would cost less than 3 mana to cost 3). Concretely, depending on how the −1 reduction is applied it will look like one of these legal final costs, but in every case the total mana you must pay is 3:
- If the reduction reduces generic mana (i.e., reduces X): with X = 0 there is no generic to reduce, so Trinisphere raises the spell to cost {1}{G}{G} (total 3). You would create 0 tokens.
- If the reduction removes one green mana symbol instead: with X = 0 you end up paying {2}{G} (two generic + one green = total 3). You would create 0 tokens.
(Those different final shapes follow the cost-reduction rules in 118.7a/118.7b/118.7c and Trinisphere ruling #0.)

3) Which X should you pick to get value? For the same three-mana outlay you can choose X = 2 and get two 1/1 Forest Dryad tokens. Reason: when you choose X = 2 the starting cost is {2}{G}{G}; after your −1 reduction this leaves a mana component of 3, so Trinisphere does not increase the cost further, and the final total you pay is still 3 mana while the spell will create X (two) tokens. Choosing X = 0 (or X = 1) makes you pay the same total 3 mana but produce fewer tokens (0 or 1), so X = 2 is the value choice for a 3-mana outlay.

Concrete short answer: If you cast Awaken the Woods with X = 0 you still must pay three mana (Trinisphere makes it cost 3) and you create 0 tokens. To get tokens for that same three-mana payment, choose X = 2 (you’ll pay three mana and get two 1/1 Forest Dryad tokens).

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes. You can target Grist in your graveyard with Animate Dead because, while it isn’t on the battlefield, Grist is a creature card as stated in the card’s ruling. When Animate Dead resolves it enters the battlefield attached to that creature card in the graveyard, then its “When this Aura enters…” ability returns the card to the battlefield and tries to attach the Aura to it (Animate Dead ruling #1; Grist ruling #1).

As soon as Grist is put onto the battlefield it is no longer a creature and is just a planeswalker (Grist ruling #1). Animate Dead’s replacement/attach attempt can’t legally attach to a noncreature permanent, so Animate Dead is put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action and its leave-the-battlefield delayed trigger is created (Animate Dead ruling #4). When that delayed triggered ability resolves, if the permanent that was returned is still on the battlefield its controller sacrifices it (Animate Dead ruling #4). State-based actions are the game rules that cause things like the Aura being put into the graveyard to happen at that time (see rule 704.4).

Net result: Grist will be returned to the battlefield, but because it becomes a planeswalker on entry Animate Dead can’t remain attached and is put into the graveyard; the resulting triggered ability will then cause you to sacrifice Grist when it resolves, so Grist will only be on the battlefield temporarily unless something else changes the situation before that trigger resolves. (Note: if Animate Dead weren’t on the battlefield when its “When this Aura enters…” triggered ability resolved, that triggered ability wouldn’t do anything; see Animate Dead ruling #0.)

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Short answer: Yes — Skullbriar keeps its four +1/+1 counters while it's in the command zone, and Doubling Season does not double those retained counters when you recast it.

Explanation and definitions:
- "Skullbriar keeps its counters as it changes zones": Skullbriar’s ability/rulings say the counters on Skullbriar remain on it as it changes zones (so the card in the command zone still has those counters) and those counters affect its power/toughness in the command zone (they are not lost). See Skullbriar rulings #1 and #3.
- "Not ‘placed’ on Skullbriar": The counters that remain on Skullbriar as it moves between zones aren’t considered to have been "placed" on it when it re-enters; they are retained. Because they aren’t being put on as it enters, replacement effects that modify how many counters are put on a permanent as it enters (for example, Doubling Season) do not affect those retained counters. Skullbriar ruling #2 explicitly states effects like Doubling Season won’t affect those counters. For context, Doubling Season does affect counters that are put on permanents as they enter (Doubling Season ruling #2), but that doesn’t apply here because the counters were retained rather than being placed as part of the enter event.

Practical result: After Skullbriar dies and you put it into the command zone with four +1/+1 counters on it, it still has those four counters in the command zone and will enter the battlefield with those same four counters when you cast it again; Doubling Season does not double them.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text:
Short answer: You do not lose the game on that extra turn. Activating Sundial of the Infinite to “end the turn” before the end step skips that turn’s end step, so Final Fortune’s “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game” won’t trigger that turn; per Sundial’s ruling those kinds of “at the beginning of the end step” triggers will instead occur at the beginning of the next turn’s end step (and Final Fortune’s ruling also notes that if an extra turn is skipped you don’t lose). Concretely: by ending the turn with Sundial before the end step, the extra turn’s end step is skipped and you don’t lose during that turn. The Final Fortune lose-trigger will not happen that turn (it will be deferred as described), and if the extra turn were entirely skipped you likewise don’t lose.

Explanation and definitions:
- “End the turn” (the expedited process that skips most of the turn and proceeds straight to the cleanup step) is what Sundial’s ability does; when a turn is ended this way the current phase/step ends and the game skips to the cleanup step, no player gets priority, and “at the beginning of the end step” triggered abilities don’t get to trigger that turn (see the rules about ending the turn and Sundial’s rulings). [724.1d] [724.1e] [724.1f] [End the Turn] [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4]
- Sundial’s official ruling: if you activate it before the end step, any “at the beginning of the end step” triggered abilities won’t get the chance to trigger that turn because the end step is skipped; those abilities will trigger at the beginning of the end step of the next turn. That means Final Fortune’s lose-the-game trigger doesn’t happen on the extra turn if you end the turn before its end step. [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1]
- Final Fortune’s own ruling: if you end up skipping the extra turn that was gained, you do not lose the game. That covers the separate case where an extra turn itself is skipped entirely; you also don’t lose the game in that situation. [Final Fortune ruling #1] [Final Fortune]

What to watch for: the lose instruction from Final Fortune won’t make you lose on the extra turn if you used Sundial to end the turn before the end step. It can be deferred as described by Sundial’s ruling, so it could still cause you to lose later if it later triggers and resolves (unless something else prevents or skips that later end step).

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
Short answer: The rules you provided say the Clone’s controller makes the “as this enters” choice as Clone enters the battlefield (and that choice can name an existing creature, or you can choose not to copy), but the provided rules do not say whether an opponent may get priority or otherwise respond between that choice being made and Clone entering. I can’t answer the “can my opponent respond?” part because the rules about replacement-effect timing and priority/when players may respond are not included in the material you gave.

What the provided rules do say (definitions and facts you can act on):
- Definition — an “as [this] enters the battlefield” choice: a decision that must be made for an object that is entering the battlefield because of an ability that modifies how it enters (for example, choosing which creature to copy). The entering object’s controller makes that choice when the object is entering as described by the ability. [707.6] [707.2]
- When the choice is made for Clone: Clone’s controller gets to make the “as this enters” copy choice when Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of another creature. You may choose only a creature that is already on the battlefield (Clone can’t choose a creature that is entering simultaneously). You may also choose not to copy anything. Clone’s ability does not target the chosen creature. [707.6] [707.2] [Clone ruling #2] [Clone ruling #5] [Clone ruling #0]
- If other replacement effects also attempt to make the entering object a copy, the affected object’s controller chooses which replacement effect to apply. (That is relevant if multiple “becomes a copy as it enters” effects would apply.) [616.1c]

What’s missing to fully answer “can my opponent respond?”: the text you provided does not include the rules that govern the timing of applying replacement effects and exactly when players receive priority or may put things on the stack relative to making “as … enters” choices. Those timing/priority rules (the rules that say when replacement effects are applied relative to the event and when players can take actions or responses) are required to determine whether an opponent can act after the copy choice but before Clone actually exists on the battlefield. results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
Short answer: You get three lands (the original Flooded Strand’s ability plus two copies). Definition: An activated ability is an ability a player activates by paying its costs; it goes on the stack and later resolves to perform its effect. What happens and why (rules you can act on):

- You activate Flooded Strand and pay its costs (tap, pay 1 life, sacrifice the land); that puts its activated ability on the stack (Flooded Strand card text).  
- While that ability is on the stack, you activate Gogo with X = 2 targeting that ability. Gogo creates two additional instances of that activated ability on the stack (Gogo ruling #6).  
- A copy of an activated ability is an ability on the stack that copies the original ability’s characteristics and the decisions made for it (707.10). Copies use the objects that were used to pay the original ability’s costs if the copy’s effect refers to those objects (707.10b), and Gogo’s copies have the same source as the original ability (Gogo ruling #9). That means you don’t need to (and won’t) sacrifice any additional Flooded Strands for the copies.  
- Each instance (the original plus the two copies) resolves separately and each one instructs you to search your library for a Plains or Island, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle. Because each instance includes its own “then shuffle” instruction, they do not merge into a single combined search; you will perform the search-and-shuffle sequence for each instance (701.23h).  

Therefore, assuming there are three eligible cards available in your library, the three resolving instances will put three lands onto the battlefield.
